title: CDN (Content Delivery Network) — caches static content (images, CSS, JS, video) at edge servers close to users, reduces latency and origin server load.

s1_definition.profdef: A content delivery network is a geographically distributed network of edge servers that cache static and cacheable content close to end users, so requests are served from a nearby edge rather than the distant origin. This reduces latency, cuts origin server load and bandwidth cost, improves availability, and absorbs traffic spikes. Caching behaviour is governed by time-to-live, cache keys, and invalidation, and content can be secured with signed URLs.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India's main data centre is in one city, but customers are everywhere. If Rajesh in Bengaluru downloads the bank's app logo and statement PDFs from that one distant data centre every time, it is slow and overloads the centre. Instead the bank keeps copies of these unchanging files in small storage rooms in every city. Rajesh gets the logo from the Bengaluru room instantly, and the main data centre barely notices. Those local storage rooms are CDN edge servers.
s1_definition.oneliner: Cache static content at edge servers near users so it loads fast and the origin is spared, controlling freshness with TTL and invalidation.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A content delivery network is a geographically distributed network of edge servers that cache static and cacheable content close to end users, so requests are served from a nearby edge rather than the distant origin. This reduces latency, cuts origin server load and bandwidth cost, improves availability, and absorbs traffic spikes. Caching behaviour is governed by time-to-live, cache keys, and invalidation, and content can be secured with signed URLs.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India's main data centre is in one city, but customers are everywhere. If Rajesh in Bengaluru downloads the bank's app logo and statement PDFs from that one distant data centre every time, it is slow and overloads the centre. Instead the bank keeps copies of these unchanging files in small storage rooms in every city. Rajesh gets the logo from the Bengaluru room instantly, and the main data centre barely notices. Those local storage rooms are CDN edge servers.

**One line to remember:** Cache static content at edge servers near users so it loads fast and the origin is spared, controlling freshness with TTL and invalidation.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's app loads the same logo, stylesheet, and help images for millions of customers, and serving each download from the central origin made the app slow for distant customers and overloaded the origin. The real problem is distance and repeated identical downloads. This is exactly what edge caching with a time-to-live solves.

Problem 2 — the bank redesigns its logo, but customers keep seeing the old one cached at the edges. The real problem is stale content after an update. This is exactly what versioned URLs and invalidation solve.

Problem 3 — the bank must never cache Rajesh's personal statement where another customer could receive it from a shared edge. The real problem is personalized content on a shared cache. This is exactly why dynamic content is excluded or isolated by cache key and secured with signed URLs.

We build a runnable CDN simulation: an `Origin` server, an `EdgeServer` with a TTL cache and miss-to-origin fetch, and a `Cdn` routing requests to the nearest edge, plus versioned URLs and invalidation. The demo serves a static logo (first a miss then hits), updates it via a versioned URL, invalidates a path, and refuses to cache a personalized statement.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is static files in the origin, two edge servers, repeated logo requests, a versioned new logo, a CSS update with invalidation, and a personalized statement request.

Step 1: Rajesh's first logo request hits the Bengaluru edge, which has nothing cached, so it fetches from the origin once, caches the result with a sixty-second time-to-live, and returns it. The origin is touched exactly once.

Step 2: Rajesh's second identical request is served from the edge cache as a hit, with no origin fetch, which is why origin load drops so much under repeated demand.

Step 3: The bank publishes a new logo under a versioned path. Because it is a brand-new URL, the edge has no cached copy and fetches it fresh, so customers never see a stale old logo and no purge was needed.

Step 4: The CSS file changes at the origin, and the CDN invalidates that path across all edges. The next request for the CSS on any edge misses and fetches the updated bytes. Finally, the personalized statement is requested via the dynamic path, which bypasses the edge cache entirely and always goes to the origin, so one customer's statement can never be served from a shared edge to another.

```
2026-11-01 00:30:00 [INFO] ORIGIN fetch /static/logo-v1.png
2026-11-01 00:30:00 [INFO] edge-bengaluru MISS->cached /static/logo-v1.png
2026-11-01 00:30:00 [INFO] edge-bengaluru HIT /static/logo-v1.png
2026-11-01 00:30:00 [INFO] ORIGIN fetch /static/logo-v2.png
2026-11-01 00:30:00 [WARNING] edge-mumbai invalidated /static/app.css
2026-11-01 00:30:00 [INFO] ORIGIN fetch /api/statement/SAV2001
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Rajesh (Bengaluru) GET /static/logo-v1.png
    │ routed to nearest edge
    ▼
  edge-bengaluru
    │
    ├─ cache MISS                      ├─ cache HIT (req2)
    │  origin.fetch (far, slow)        │  serve locally (fast)
    │  cache with TTL 60s              │
    ▼                                  ▼
  bytes + cached                     bytes (no origin touch)

  new logo → versioned URL /logo-v2.png → fresh fetch (no staleness)

  CSS changed at origin
    │ Cdn.invalidate("/static/app.css") → purge all edges
    ▼
  next request MISS → origin → updated bytes

  personalized /api/statement/SAV2001
    │ getDynamic → bypass edges → ALWAYS origin (no cross-user leak)
    ▼
  per-user content from origin
```

  1. cdn.get("edge-bengaluru", "/static/logo-v1.png")
  2.   → edge.serve → cache miss → origin.fetch → cache.put
  3. cdn.get(... same ...)
  4.   → edge.serve → cache HIT → return (no origin)

sections.s6_takeaway:
A content delivery network is a geographically distributed set of edge servers that cache static, cacheable content close to end users, so a request is served from a nearby edge instead of the distant origin. The fundamental benefit is proximity: network latency grows with distance, so serving a file from an edge a few milliseconds away rather than an origin hundreds of milliseconds away makes an app feel instant, while simultaneously sparing the origin and cutting bandwidth cost.

The mechanism is caching with a time-to-live. When an edge lacks a requested file, it fetches it from the origin once, stores it, and serves all subsequent requests from its cache until the time-to-live expires. That is why origin load drops so dramatically: instead of serving the same logo to millions of users, the origin serves it once per edge per expiry period. At National Bank of India, this is exactly what fixed slow app loads for distant customers, because the logo, stylesheet, and help images came from a nearby edge rather than the central data centre.

Keeping content fresh is the next concern. The cache key, usually the URL, decides what counts as the same object, and I am careful never to let a cache key accidentally serve one user's personalized content to another. When a file changes, I prefer versioned URLs, giving the updated file a new name so clients simply request a fresh, uncached object, which avoids the delay and cost of purging. When I must purge, I issue an explicit invalidation to remove the path from all edges. Crucially, I only cache content that is identical for every user, like images, scripts, and video segments, and I keep dynamic personalized content such as a specific account balance off the edge entirely, or isolate it with a very short time-to-live and a per-user cache key.

The senior points I always raise are security and resilience. Premium or private content is protected with signed, time-limited URLs so only authorized users can fetch it, which matters for a bank serving confidential documents. And because the CDN's distributed edge network can absorb volumetric traffic far better than a single origin, it doubles as denial-of-service protection and even accelerates API traffic. That combination of edge proximity, TTL caching, versioned invalidation, careful handling of personalized content, and signed URLs is what makes a CDN both fast and safe in a production banking system.
